evidence.source: Academia Sinica Institute of History and Philology, Chinese Character Knowledge Database
evidence.text: The database describes the old graph as a hand holding a shell, representing obtaining; 彳 may be added to show an action. It lists senses including obtain/acquire and extended senses such as meet, use, understand, finish, suffice, reach, be able, and auxiliary/particle functions. This page does not date individual sense extensions or establish their sequence.

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Xiaoxuetang Oracle Bone Database
evidence.text: The database reports 2,548 oracle-bone head characters and 24,701 forms as of 2026-09-26. Its search page is accessible, but the inspected page did not return a character-specific 得 entry or inscription examples.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry treats 䙷 as an old form of 得 and relates 䙷 to 㝵 as a variant; its note summarizes Shuowen entries distinguishing 䙷 ‘take’ under 見 and 得 ‘obtain in movement’ under 彳. It explains 得 as 彳 plus 䙷 as phonetic, but the text also describes a historical development from a graph for taking to one with 彳. This supports variant/old-form connections but does not by itself establish the complete chronology of the paleographic shapes.
evidence.title: [A01291-013] 䙷 (得) — Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: 漢語國學, online Shuowen text and commentary
evidence.text: The page gives the Shuowen definition 行有所得也。从彳䙷聲 and cites Duan Yucai's correction of 得 to 㝵 in the definition. Its modern paleographic account describes oracle-bone forms as 又/爪 holding 貝, optional 彳, Chu forms with 貝 rendered as 目, Qin forms replacing 又 with 寸, and later clerical transformation of the relevant form toward 旦. It reports the account that the Shuowen seal shape resembling 見 may be a corruption of 貝. These are the page's scholarly/editorial assertions, not independently verified inspection of glyph images in this research.
evidence.title: 得的说文解字解释

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project, Shuowen Jiezi, 見部
evidence.text: The Shuowen text records 䙷 as 取也 (‘take/acquire’) and analyzes it as 見 plus 寸, explaining 寸 as a measure and also a hand. This is Xu Shen's Han-period lexicographic analysis, not direct confirmation of an earlier inscriptional form.
evidence.title: Shuo Wen Jie Zi: 卷九: 見部

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project, Shuowen Jiezi via the inspected Shuowen commentary page
evidence.text: The Shuowen entry is transmitted as 行有所得也。从彳㝵聲, ‘in travel/movement, to have something obtained; from 彳, with 㝵 as phonetic’. Duan Yucai's commentary says copies reading 得 in the definition should be corrected to 㝵 and notes 䙷 in the 見部 as ‘take’. This source assertion explicitly supports a phonetic role for 㝵/䙷 within 得, independently of uncertainty about the depicted shell's name.
evidence.title: 得的说文解字解释

evidence.text: The page labels oracle forms approximately 1250–1000 BCE, late Shang bronze forms approximately 1100 BCE, Shuowen seal forms around 100 CE, and Eastern Han clerical forms 25–220 CE. It describes 得 as ‘obtain’ and separately lists Mandarin dé, de, and děi senses. The page shows no dated textual attestations for these lexical extensions, and its paleographic dates are page assertions rather than a character-specific inscriptional catalogue consulted here.
evidence.title: 得 — Dong Chinese dictionary

evidence.text: The entry presents 得 as an ideogrammic compound from ancient 㝵 (貝 + 又), with 彳 sometimes added; it asserts Qin-script 又-to-寸 replacement, possible Shuowen corruption of 貝 toward 見, clerical 貝-to-目 reduction, and later 目-to-旦 change. These specific script-history claims are secondary assertions and are not fully corroborated by the primary database records inspected in this run.
evidence.title: 得 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: The page reports Pulleyblank (1991) as relating 得 to Tibetan ཐུབ thub ‘be able; withstand’, while marking the etymology incomplete. The page provides no argument or documentation here sufficient to establish a borrowing or cognate relationship; this remains disputed/unverified.
evidence.title: 得 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: For 得 dé ‘obtain’, the database gives Middle Chinese tok and Old Chinese *tˤək (2014 system; GSR 0905d). This establishes the character's reconstructed reading in that system, not the pronunciation of a depicted shell/object and not on its own the phonetic role of 㝵.

evidence.text: 得 is listed as Old Chinese *tɯːɡ in the Zhengzhang system and Middle Chinese tok in Baxter's notation. These are system-specific reconstructions for 得, not independently verified reconstructions of 㝵 in this research.

evidence.text: Modern Standard Mandarin is dé (Pinyin); standard Cantonese is dak1 (Jyutping). These readings show modern forms but do not establish an ancient object-name or loan source.

evidence.source: 漢語國學, online Shuowen text and commentary
evidence.text: The commentary classifies the hand-holding-shell configuration as an ideographic alternative, and the graph with 彳 plus 䙷/㝵 as phonetic and also semantically suggestive. On this account 彳 is a semantic component associated with movement; 䙷/㝵 is the phonetic base. It treats 䙷 and 㝵 as graph variants in the historical lexicographic tradition. This supports origin_relation=variant_form for a component record that distinguishes 㝵 from the component form 䙷; it does not prove a chronological ancestry from one graphic shape to the other.

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction database
evidence.text: The inspected Baxter–Sagart table gives 得 as *tˤək but did not provide a verified entry for the particular 㝵 component form. Since component-specific pronunciation was not independently established from this inspected table, the shared sound relation rests on Shuowen's explicit 聲 analysis, rather than a demonstrated pair of component and compound reconstructions.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1

evidence.field: form analysis and dated usage examples
evidence.text: The database interprets early 得 forms as 貝 plus a hand element 又 (with other hand forms also attested), sometimes with 彳 to suggest getting shell currency while travelling. It cites oracle-bone 《合集》8928 ‘弗其得’, bronze 《懷特》359 ‘得馬’, and the Zhongshan King square pot phrase ‘敄(務)才(在)得賢’. It says later forms sometimes reshape 貝 toward 目 or 日, the received small-seal form toward 見, and 又 toward 寸. These are the database’s paleographic interpretation; individual artifacts and images were not inspected in this run.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 得

evidence.text: The database transmits the Shuowen 彳部 entry as 行有所得也。从彳，㝵聲 and records 多則切; it also gives the 見部 gloss for 㝵 as 取也 with the analysis 从見从寸. This explicitly supports the historical lexicographic claim that 㝵/䙷 functions as a phonetic element within 得, regardless of uncertainty about the ancient referent or name of the shell-like part.

It presents an account in which 彳 was added to a pre-existing 䙷 graph. This supports variant_form, not an independently verified chronological sequence among all paleographic shapes.

evidence.text: The displayed Duan Yucai note corrects the transmitted Shuowen definition from 得 to 㝵, compares 䙷 ‘take’ in the 見部, and reads the 彳部 entry as ‘in movement, to obtain something’; it explicitly analyzes 得 as 彳 plus phonetic 䙷 and gives 多則切. It also calls 㝵 an ancient graph with 彳 omitted. This is a Qing commentary on a Han lexicographic account, not direct confirmation of the original inscriptional referent.

evidence.field: pre-Qin corpus analysis and semantic history
evidence.text: The 2010 abstract reports quantitative and qualitative analysis of 1,319 occurrences of 得 in six pre-Qin texts. The author argues that forms with nominal or predicate complements in those texts remain transitive ‘obtain/acquire’ uses, and that an auxiliary use had not yet developed in the pre-Qin period. This is a scholarly analysis, not a consensus statement; it conflicts with other published descriptions that date a possibility use to pre-Qin.

evidence.text: The database cites several Warring States bamboo texts using 得 in contexts translated or interpreted as obtain/get, including Guodian Laozi ‘不貴難得之貨’ and Qinghua Xinian ‘得師以來’. The cited examples establish these uses by the period represented by those manuscripts; they do not date every later modal, resultative, or particle function.

gaps: No dated, character-specific oracle-bone inscription for 得 was individually verified here. Database query and paleographic image access did not yield an inspected 得 record, so an earliest attestation date cannot be confidently supplied.

No continuous dated series of bronze, Warring States, seal, clerical, and regular forms was inspected directly. Specific accounts of 貝→目/旦, 又→寸, and a Shuowen 貝→見 corruption remain attributed to secondary commentary and disputed or incompletely corroborated.

The dossier's apparent component issue is unresolved: Shuowen explicitly calls 㝵 a phonetic in 得, while some modern accounts describe the initial 貝+又 graph as an ideographic compound and later 彳 as added. The evidence allows both graphic/semantic history and phonetic role in the later compound to be reported separately; it does not establish when 㝵 became phonetic or the exact original relation of all shapes.

Pronunciation comparison is incomplete for 㝵:得 has verified Baxter–Sagart *tˤək and Zhengzhang *tɯːɡ, but this research did not recover a corresponding component-specific reconstruction for 㝵. Therefore the formal phonetic claim follows the explicit Shuowen account, not a demonstrated reconstruction match.

No primary, dated corpus survey established the chronology of extended senses such as meet, understand, be able, must, or grammatical particle uses. Dictionary gloss sequences are not treated as semantic chronology.

Pulleyblank's proposed relation to Tibetan ཐུབ was found only as a secondary report; the source-word history, sound correspondences, and early attestations were not independently verified, so no borrowing conclusion is warranted.

No evidence supports identifying or reconstructing the ancient name/pronunciation of the shell/cowry object. The hand-and-shell interpretation is a graphic-semantic explanation; any separate phonetic claim does not depend on assuming a recoverable shell name.

The ancient shell/cowry interpretation is an account of graphic-semantic composition. No inspected source establishes the object’s original name or pronunciation, so no separate loan claim based on the shell’s name is made.

The phonetic role of 㝵/䙷 in 得 is explicitly asserted by the Shuowen tradition, but this research did not recover an independently verified Baxter–Sagart or Zhengzhang reconstruction for the component form; do not claim a measured reconstruction match.

The transmission of the Shuowen seal form resembling 見 and the later 貝-to-目/日/旦 graphic accounts are not fully settled. CUHK describes variants and potential misreadings, but direct dated examples spanning the entire transition were not individually inspected.

The corpus study and some modern dictionaries disagree about whether an auxiliary/modal use was already present in pre-Qin texts. The KCI abstract reports an analysis of 1,319 examples and argues that the uses still mean ‘obtain’; exact chronology of later auxiliary, resultative, and particle functions remains disputed.

The reported Pulleyblank comparison of 得 with Tibetan ཐུབ thub was not independently verified; source-word history, sound correspondences, early attestations, and borrowing direction remain unresolved.

A Palace Museum search result reported particular oracle and bronze examples (including 《合集》8928 and named bronzes), but its linked PDF timed out on inspection. CUHK’s page independently cites the 《合集》 example, but artifact images and reading details were not inspected directly.

The Sinica site labels oracle, bronze, Chu-slip/silk, and small-seal forms, but its image endpoint returned a cache miss and no individual Sinica glyph pixels were visually inspected. Commons files are modern vector redrawings based on cited source material, not artifact photography.

The 㝵 silk-style Wikimedia Commons candidate appeared in search, but opening its file page returned a cache miss, so its rights and provenance were not independently confirmed in this run. The selected candidates are the oracle and bronze redrawings, whose pages explicitly identify sources and public-domain/CC0 terms.

The seal-style Commons file is a usable identity candidate but carries both a public-domain declaration and a metadata note referring to Richard Sears copyright and permission; that wording is internally ambiguous, so its reuse status should be independently resolved before use.

The oracle vector's direct URL is recorded from the Commons page's actual Original file link, but the web tool could not fetch/render SVG content; the page description and rights were inspected, not the glyph pixels.

The bronze file has an indexed description supporting identity and public-domain status, but its Commons page could not be reopened and no actual direct image URL was recovered. Excluded from candidates until a verified direct URL is available.
No image pixels were visually inspected in this stage. Both proposed descriptions explicitly identify modern vector redrawings rather than ancient artifact photographs.
